content: Additional therapeutic interventions are recommended for children living with HIV who are also diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB). These include co-trimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT), early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), pyridoxine supplementation, and nutritional support. Co-trimoxazole is a broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent that helps prevent secondary bacterial and parasitic infections in individuals with HIV. Daily prophylaxis with CPT has been shown to improve survival rates in children with HIV, reduce the incidence of co-morbidities, and lower the risk of opportunistic infections such as pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV-exposed infants. Consequently, CPT is recommended for all HIV-exposed infants and children living with HIV, including those with TB, as part of a comprehensive HIV care package. The initiation, discontinuation, and monitoring of CPT are guided by the 2006 WHO guidelines on co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for HIV-related infections. ART in children with HIV aims to enhance both the quality and length of life by reducing HIV-related morbidity and mortality. It achieves this by decreasing the incidence of opportunistic infections, lowering viral load, restoring and preserving immune function, and supporting normal growth and development. ART has also been shown to improve TB treatment outcomes in children with HIV. The WHO recommends ART for all individuals with confirmed HIV infection and a CD4 count of ≤500 cells/mm³, with priority given to those with advanced HIV disease or a CD4 count of ≤350 cells/mm³. ART should also be initiated in individuals with active TB, hepatitis B virus (HBV) co-infection with severe liver disease, all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV, all children under five years of age with HIV, and individuals in serodiscordant relationships, regardless of CD4 count. For children with TB, TB treatment should be initiated first, followed by ART as soon as possible, ideally within eight weeks of starting TB treatment. For those with a CD4 count below 50 cells/mm³, ART should be initiated within two weeks of starting TB treatment. For first-line ART regimens, simplified and less toxic combinations, preferably as fixed-dose formulations, are recommended for their effectiveness and convenience. For children older than three years, regimens typically include a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone (e.g., tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [TDF] or abacavir [ABC] with lamivudine [3TC]) combined with a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) such as efavirenz (EFV). For children younger than three years, a protease inhibitor (PI)-based regimen, such as lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) combined with ABC or zidovudine (AZT), is preferred. When treating children with TB who are already on ART, the choice of ART regimen must be compatible with TB therapy. Interactions between rifampicin and certain ART drugs, such as LPV/r or nevirapine (NVP), pose challenges, particularly in children under three years of age. In such cases, triple NRTI regimens (e.g., AZT + 3TC + ABC) may be considered as a suitable option during TB treatment. For children older than three years, EFV-based regimens are preferred. If a child is on NVP, switching to EFV or a triple NRTI regimen is recommended. For children on PI-based regimens, adjustments such as adding ritonavir (RTV) to achieve full therapeutic dosing may be necessary. Adherence to ART in children presents unique challenges due to factors such as limited pediatric formulations, poor palatability of liquid formulations, high pill or liquid volume burden, large pill sizes, frequent dosing requirements, dietary restrictions, loss of primary caregivers, difficulties swallowing tablets, and adverse effects. Successful treatment requires the commitment and involvement of a responsible caregiver. Suboptimal HIV care for family members can negatively impact the care of the child. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is a temporary clinical deterioration that may occur within three months of starting ART, most commonly within the first month. It results from the restoration of cell-mediated immunity in response to mycobacterial antigens and can mimic worsening TB disease, presenting with fever and enlarged lymph nodes or tuberculomas. Risk factors for IRIS include low baseline CD4 count, extensive TB, early ART initiation, and rapid immunological and virological responses to ART. While IRIS can cause significant morbidity, it is not associated with increased mortality. In cases of TB-IRIS, anti-TB treatment should be continued, and corticosteroids may be considered in some cases. For children with drug-resistant TB (DR-TB), every effort should be made to confirm the diagnosis through culture and drug susceptibility testing (DST). Rapid DST for isoniazid and rifampicin, or rifampicin alone, is preferred over conventional testing due to its ability to provide results within hours to days, enabling earlier treatment initiation and improved outcomes. In confirmed cases of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), second-line DST should be performed to exclude extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) and guide effective treatment regimens. Preventive therapy for contacts of DR-TB patients is not currently recommended by WHO due to a lack of clinical trial data. However, all children with an infectious TB contact should be screened for TB disease, particularly those living with HIV or in households with DR-TB cases. Close follow-up of asymptomatic children is essential, with regular monitoring every 2–3 months for the first six months and then every six months for at least two years.
